intro: By now you have read the major traditions one at a time: the Torah and the prophets, the Gospels and Paul, the Qur'an and the Hadith, the Upanishads and the Gita, the Dhammapada, the Analects and the Daodejing, the Guru Granth Sahib, and traditions carried in story and ceremony. This unit turns the course sideways. Instead of asking what one tradition teaches, it asks a single human question and lets each tradition answer it in its own words.

The questions are the oldest ones. How should a person live, and what do people owe one another? What happens when we die, and why is there suffering at all? Every student in the room already has some answer, from a family, a congregation, a book or their own thinking. Reading the traditions side by side shows where their answers meet, such as the Golden Rule and care for the poor. It also shows where they part, over God, the self and what comes after death.

By the end of the unit you will be able to set two or three sacred texts beside each other, attribute each teaching to its tradition, explain the reason each text gives, and show the variety inside a tradition as well as the differences between them. You will practice the discipline at the heart of this course: comparing carefully, in the traditions' own terms, without declaring a winner.
bigQuestion: When the world's traditions answer the same great questions, what do they share, where do they differ, and why?

title: One Question, Many Lenses

chapters.title: What Is a Good Life? What Is Justice?
chapters.bigQuestion: When the world's traditions answer the question of how to live well and fairly, where do their answers meet and where do they part?

story.title: One Question on the Board
story.kicker: A teacher writes seven words on a whiteboard, and six students discover that they have each been handed an answer before they ever heard the question.
paragraphs: The teacher wrote the question in blue marker and capped the pen: What is a good life, and what is justice? Then she asked six volunteers to answer, not from their opinions, but from a text their family or community treats as sacred, or from a philosopher if they had no such text. She gave them ten minutes and a stack of library copies. The room got quiet in the way a room does when people realize the assignment is harder than it looked.

Miriam found the passage in Leviticus that her grandfather quoted at every holiday meal, about loving your neighbor as yourself, and then a line from the prophet Micah about doing justice and loving mercy. Daniel opened Matthew to the Sermon on the Mount and read the Beatitudes twice, once for the words and once for the order. Yusuf asked whether he could bring in a verse from the Qur'an about standing firm for justice even against your own family. The teacher said that was exactly the point.

Priya had a copy of the Bhagavad Gita that had belonged to her aunt. She marked the lines in which Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna to do his duty without grasping at the reward. Kenji, whose grandmother kept a small Buddhist altar, wrote out the eight steps of the path and circled three of them: right speech, right action, right livelihood. Marcus said his family was not religious, so he went to the philosophy shelf and came back with Aristotle and a slim book by John Stuart Mill.

When the six read their answers aloud, something unexpected happened. Nobody had said the same thing, but nobody had said something the others found strange. Miriam's neighbor and Daniel's enemy-love and Yusuf's justice and Priya's duty and Kenji's right speech and Marcus's greatest happiness all seemed to be looking at the same mountain from different trails. Then Kenji asked whether the trails really led to the same place. Priya said the Gita and the Dhammapada disagreed about whether there is a self at all, so how could they agree about a good life for it?

The teacher did not answer. She uncapped the marker, drew a table with six columns, and said that the rest of the chapter would be spent filling it in. The rule was simple. Every answer had to be attributed to a text and a tradition, every belief had to be described rather than judged, and no column was allowed to be declared the winner. The bell rang before anyone had written a word, and six students walked out arguing in the hall.
story.think: The six answers seemed alike until someone pressed on the details. Why might the surface of an ethical teaching look similar across traditions while the reasoning underneath differs?

lessons.title: Two Questions, Not One
lessons.mainIdea: A good life asks what a person should become; justice asks what people owe one another, and every tradition answers both.
reading: Look again at the sentence on the whiteboard. It contains two questions that people often blur together. What is a good life? is a question about a single person: what habits, aims and character make a human life go well. What is justice? is a question about relationships: what one person owes another, what a ruler owes the ruled, what a community owes the stranger at its gate. A tradition can answer one without saying much about the other, and the differences between traditions often show up in how they connect the two.

Scholars call the study of these questions *ethics*, from the Greek word for character or custom. Religious ethics is ethics grounded in a tradition's texts, practices and picture of the world. When the Torah commands Israel to leave the corners of a field unharvested for the poor, it is answering the justice question. When the Buddha describes a mind free of craving, he is answering the good-life question. Most sacred texts do both, and often in the same passage.

This chapter reads each tradition's answer in its own words before it compares anything. That order matters. A comparison built on summaries tends to flatten every teaching into the same shape, and then the comparison proves nothing. A comparison built on texts, with the reasoning attached, lets real agreements and real differences show. By the end you should be able to state what a tradition teaches about living well, name the text it comes from, and explain the reason that text gives.

Notice what the chapter does not do. It does not decide which answer is correct. In a public school, the academic study of religion describes what adherents believe and why, attributes each claim to its source, and leaves the judgment to the student and the family. That restraint is not a weakness of the method. It is what lets a Jewish student, a Muslim student and a student with no religion read the same page and each find it fair.

Two of these speak mainly to justice between people; two speak mainly to the inner shape of a good life.

lessons.title: Comparing Without Ranking
lessons.mainIdea: Fair comparison describes each tradition in its own terms, attributes every claim, shows variety within the tradition, and refuses to declare a winner.
reading: In 1893 the World's Parliament of Religions met in Chicago, on the lakefront where the Art Institute now stands. For seventeen days in September, representatives of Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Judaism, Islam, Christianity in many forms, and other traditions spoke from the same platform. It is often described as the first large gathering of its kind. Some speakers used the stage to argue that their own faith was best. Others, like the Hindu monk Swami Vivekananda, argued that the traditions should learn from one another. Both impulses are still with us, and this chapter chooses the second, in an academic form.

Fair comparison follows a few rules. First, describe each tradition in the terms its own scholars and adherents use: dharma rather than "Hindu law," mitzvah rather than "Jewish rule." Second, attribute every claim, so that a sentence reports what a text says rather than asserting that it is so. Third, show *diversity within* the tradition; Sunni and Shia Muslims, or Orthodox and Reform Jews, may read the same verse differently, and a description that hides this is inaccurate. Fourth, do not rank. A student may hold private views, but the comparison itself stays neutral.

There is a fifth rule that is easy to forget: compare like with like. Setting a tradition's highest ideal against another tradition's worst failure is a common trick, and it proves nothing. If you compare the Sermon on the Mount with Islamic teaching, compare it with the Qur'an's teaching on mercy, not with a headline. If you compare Buddhist compassion with Judaism, compare it with the prophets, not with a stereotype. The table the teacher drew has six columns, and every column gets the same kind of entry: a text, a teaching and a reason.

One more thing before the reading starts. Sizes differ. Christianity and Islam together count more than half the world's people; Sikhism counts perhaps thirty million; Jainism a few million; the traditions of many Indigenous peoples count in the thousands. A tradition's size says nothing about the depth or interest of its answer, and this chapter gives each answer room. The data below shows why the comparison cannot be settled by counting heads.

lessons.title: The Torah's Neighbor
lessons.mainIdea: In Jewish tradition the good life is a life of mitzvot, and justice begins with the command to love the neighbor and protect the stranger, the widow and the poor.
reading: In the middle of Leviticus, among rules about harvests and honest scales, stands one sentence. Jewish tradition has treated it as a summary of the whole law: you shall love your neighbor as yourself. The verse (Leviticus 19:18) does not float free. It ends a list of concrete commands. Do not steal. Do not lie. Do not hold back a worker's wages overnight. Do not curse the deaf. Do not favor either the poor or the powerful in court. Love of neighbor, in the Torah's way of speaking, is a set of actions before it is a feeling.

The Hebrew word for one of these commands is *mitzvah*, plural mitzvot. Rabbinic tradition counts 613 of them in the Torah, ranging from Sabbath rest to returning a lost animal. To live a good life, in this understanding, is to live inside the *covenant*, the binding agreement between God and Israel made at Sinai, by keeping the commandments. The Ten Commandments (Exodus 20) are the best known, but Jewish teachers have always stressed that they are a beginning, not the whole.

Justice in the Torah has a particular shape. Again and again the text names three vulnerable figures, the stranger, the orphan and the widow, and ties their protection to Israel's own memory: you were strangers in Egypt. Farmers must leave the corners of the field and the fallen grain for the poor (Leviticus 19:9–10). Every seventh year debts are released. The Hebrew word *tzedakah*, which came to mean giving to the poor, shares its root with the word for justice. In Jewish thought, giving is not charity in the sense of an optional kindness; it is owed.

Jews do not all read these laws the same way. Orthodox Jews hold that the commandments bind in full and that rabbinic interpretation over centuries defines how. Reform Judaism, which took shape in nineteenth-century Germany and America, treats the ethical commands as central and many ritual commands as matters of informed choice. Conservative Judaism stands between. Yet across these movements, the phrase from Leviticus and the prophets' demand for justice remain the common ground, and the story of the Exodus remains the reason: a people freed from slavery is commanded to remember what it was like.

lessons.title: The Prophets Demand Justice
lessons.mainIdea: Amos, Micah and Isaiah taught that worship without justice for the poor is worthless, giving Judaism and Christianity a shared language for social ethics.
reading: Around 750 BCE a herdsman named Amos walked north from Judah to the sanctuary at Bethel in the kingdom of Israel and began to shout. The kingdom was prosperous, its festivals crowded, its altars busy. Amos said that none of it mattered. In the words of the King James Version, God says, "I hate, I despise your feast days," and then demands instead that judgment run down like water and righteousness like a mighty stream (Amos 5:21–24). The offense Amos names is specific: the rich sell the poor for a pair of shoes, cheat with false weights and crush the needy in court.

A *prophet*, in the Hebrew Bible, is not mainly a predictor of the future. The word means one who speaks for another, and the prophets speak for God to a people who have, in their view, broken the covenant. Their charge is nearly always the same: the powerful have forgotten the poor, the widow and the stranger, and ritual cannot cover it. Isaiah asks what use are sacrifices when hands are full of blood, and tells the people to seek justice and defend the orphan (Isaiah 1:11–17). Micah compresses the whole message into one line, quoted below.

This prophetic tradition shaped both Judaism and Christianity. In synagogues the prophets are read each Sabbath after the Torah portion, in a reading called the *haftarah*, and Reform Judaism in particular has made the prophets' social justice central to its identity. In churches, Jesus is shown quoting Isaiah at the start of his ministry (Luke 4), and Christian movements from abolition to the civil rights movement have preached from Amos. Martin Luther King Jr. quoted Amos 5:24 in his speech at the March on Washington in 1963.

Read carefully, the prophets are not against worship. Amos and Isaiah assume the festivals and sacrifices will continue. Their claim is that worship and justice are one system, and that a community cannot keep the first half while breaking the second. That claim, that how you treat the poor is a religious matter and not only a political one, is one of the Hebrew Bible's distinctive contributions to the question on the board.

lessons.title: The Sermon on the Mount
lessons.mainIdea: In Matthew 5–7 Jesus blesses the poor and the merciful, commands love of enemies, and gives the Golden Rule, which Christians read as the shape of life in the Kingdom of God.
reading: The Gospel of Matthew gathers a long stretch of Jesus's teaching into a single scene. He climbs a hill, sits down as a teacher would, and speaks to his disciples while a crowd listens (Matthew 5–7). Christians call it the *Sermon on the Mount*. It opens with the *Beatitudes*, a series of blessings on people the world does not usually count as fortunate. They are the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers and the persecuted. Matthew lists eight or nine, depending on how they are counted. The Gospel of Luke gives a shorter set of four, paired with four warnings to the rich and the comfortable (Luke 6:20–26).

The sermon then takes up the Torah directly. Jesus says he has come not to destroy the law but to fulfill it, and six times he quotes a command and pushes it inward: not only do not kill, but do not nurse anger; not only love your neighbor, but love your enemy. The passage on enemies, quoted below, is among the most discussed lines in Christian ethics. It asks not merely for restraint but for active good toward those who do harm. Christians have read it as a personal command, as a command for churches, and, in some traditions such as the Mennonites and Quakers, as a reason to refuse all violence.

Near the end comes the sentence often called the *Golden Rule*: whatever you would have others do to you, do to them, "for this is the law and the prophets" (Matthew 7:12). That last phrase matters. Jesus is presented as summarizing the Hebrew Bible, not replacing it, and Jewish teachers of the same era, such as Hillel, taught a closely related rule. The sermon also teaches the Lord's Prayer, warns against showing off piety, and tells the listener to store treasure in heaven rather than on earth.

What is the good life in the sermon? Christians describe it as life in the *Kingdom of God*: a way of living that trusts God for tomorrow, forgives as it hopes to be forgiven, and treats mercy as the measure by which one will be measured. Christians differ on how literally its hardest lines apply. Roman Catholic teaching has often read the sermon as counsel of perfection alongside the commandments; Martin Luther read it as showing how far everyone falls short and needs grace; Anabaptists read it as a plain rule for the church. All agree that it sets the standard.

lessons.title: Justice and Mercy in the Qur'an
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an commands justice even against oneself and one's kin, pairs it with God's mercy, and makes care for the poor a pillar of the good life.
reading: Every chapter of the Qur'an but one opens with the same phrase: in the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful. Muslims recite it before meals, journeys and tasks. The two words for mercy come from the Arabic root *rahma*, related to the word for a mother's womb, and Muslim scholars have long noted that the Qur'an names God's mercy far more often than God's anger. The good life, in this picture, begins with recognizing a merciful Creator and responding with gratitude and obedience, which is what the word islam, submission, means.

Justice, *'adl* in Arabic, is commanded with unusual force. One verse tells believers to stand firm for justice as witnesses for God, even if it goes against themselves, their parents or their relatives, and whether the person concerned is rich or poor (Qur'an 4:135). Another says that hatred of a people must not push believers into injustice, because being just is closer to piety (5:8). A third, often recited at the end of Friday sermons, says that God commands justice, the doing of good and generosity to relatives, and forbids indecency, wrongdoing and oppression (16:90). Justice is not softened by mercy in these verses; the two are demanded together.

Concrete duties follow. Zakat, one of the Five Pillars, requires Muslims with savings above a threshold to give a fixed share each year, commonly reckoned at 2.5 percent, to the poor and other named categories. Beyond zakat, voluntary giving called *sadaqa* is praised throughout the Qur'an and the Hadith. Honest weights, kindness to orphans, fair treatment of workers and the release of debtors recur as marks of the righteous, often in language close to the Hebrew prophets, whom the Qur'an also honors as messengers of God.

Muslims have developed these commands into detailed law, and the schools of *sharia* differ on many particulars. Sunni scholars follow several schools and Shia scholars others. Sufi teachers have stressed the inner side of mercy and justice, the purifying of the heart. But the question on the board gets a recognizable answer across all of them. A good life is a life lived in grateful submission to a merciful God. Justice is what that God commands, without exception for the powerful or for oneself.

words.d: mercy or compassion; the root of the names of God that open nearly every chapter of the Qur'an
justice; in the Qur'an, commanded even against one's own interest and one's own family
the required yearly giving of a share of one's wealth to the poor; one of the Five Pillars of Islam
voluntary giving beyond zakat, praised in the Qur'an and the Hadith
the path of God's guidance as Muslim scholars work it out in law; several schools exist

lessons.title: Dharma and the Gita's Answer
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu traditions describe the good life as living one's dharma, and the Gita teaches that right action is done as duty and offering, without grasping at its reward.
reading: The Bhagavad Gita opens on a battlefield. The warrior Arjuna looks across at the opposing army, sees his cousins, teachers and friends, and drops his bow. He would rather be killed than kill them. His charioteer, who is the god Krishna in human form, answers him over eighteen chapters. The Gita is part of the vast epic Mahabharata, which scholars think was composed in stages over several centuries, roughly 400 BCE to 400 CE, and it has become for many Hindus the single most read statement of how to live.

The first word Krishna reaches for is *dharma*. The term has no single English equivalent. It means duty, right order, the way things are meant to go, and the responsibilities of a person's role and stage of life. Arjuna is a warrior. Krishna tells him that a warrior's dharma is to fight a just war, and that shrinking from it out of grief is a failure of duty. Hindu ethics has always held that duties differ by role: a student's dharma is not a householder's, and a ruler's is not a priest's. Historically this idea was tied to the caste system. Modern reformers since the nineteenth century, including many devout Hindus, have argued that the ethical core of dharma can be kept while the hereditary hierarchy is rejected.

Krishna's most famous teaching answers the good-life question directly. You have a right to your actions, he says, but never to the fruits of your actions; do your duty because it is your duty, and let go of the craving for reward. In Edwin Arnold's 1885 verse translation, the counsel is to find full reward of doing right in right itself. This is *karma yoga*, the path of action without attachment. Krishna adds two more paths: jnana yoga, the path of knowledge, in which one realizes that the true self is not the body; and *bhakti yoga*, the path of loving devotion to God, which many readers, though not all, take the Gita finally to name as the highest.

How does this bear on justice? The Gita's picture is that a person acting from duty rather than self-interest becomes a steady point in the world, doing what the role requires and offering the result to God. Gandhi, who read the Gita daily, drew from it a discipline of selfless service and, unlike many earlier readers, a commitment to nonviolence. Other Hindus have drawn from the same text a defense of a warrior's duty. Both readings exist within the tradition, and a fair account names them both.

the path of action performed as duty, without attachment to its results
the path of loving devotion to God, which many readers see the Gita presenting as the highest
the great Sanskrit epic of a war between cousins, of which the Bhagavad Gita is a part

look.text: Krishna tells Arjuna that his concern is with action alone, never with its fruits. He should not act for the sake of reward, but neither should he cling to inaction. look.prompt: Imagine a student who studies hard only when a grade is at stake, and one who studies the same way whether or not it counts. Which is closer to Krishna's counsel, and what does the Gita think the second student gains?

lessons.title: The Eightfold Path and Compassion
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists describe the good life as walking the Eightfold Path, whose ethical steps are right speech, right action and right livelihood, and whose fruit is compassion for all beings.
reading: The Buddha's first teaching, as tradition records it, was given to five companions in a deer park near Varanasi. He laid out Four Noble Truths: life as ordinarily lived involves dukkha, suffering or unsatisfactoriness; its cause is craving; it can end; and the way to its end is the *Eightfold Path*. The path is the Buddhist answer to the good-life question, and it is a practice rather than a creed. Its eight parts are right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration.

Buddhist teachers group the eight into three trainings. Wisdom covers view and intention; concentration covers effort, mindfulness and meditation; and *sila*, ethical conduct, covers speech, action and livelihood. This middle group is where justice lives. Right speech means no lying, no slander, no harsh words, no idle chatter. Right action is spelled out in the Five Precepts that lay Buddhists undertake: to refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech and intoxicants. Right livelihood rules out trades that harm, and early texts name dealing in weapons, living beings, meat, intoxicants and poisons.

What ties ethics to the rest of the path is the claim that harm and craving are linked. The Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse, opens by saying that all we are is the result of what we have thought. A mind full of hatred produces harmful acts and further suffering; a mind trained toward *metta*, loving-kindness, and *karuna*, compassion, produces the opposite. Buddhists cultivate these deliberately in meditation, extending goodwill first to oneself, then to friends, then to strangers, then to enemies, then to all beings.

Across Buddhist schools the emphasis shifts. Theravada Buddhism, strong in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, stresses the individual's discipline on the path. Mahayana Buddhism, dominant in East Asia, holds up the *bodhisattva*, one who delays final liberation to help all beings, and makes compassion the highest ideal. Engaged Buddhists in the twentieth century, such as the Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh, applied the precepts to war, poverty and the environment. In all of these, the good life and justice are the same training seen from inside and from outside.

ethical conduct; the part of the path made up of right speech, right action and right livelihood
loving-kindness, goodwill toward all beings, cultivated in Buddhist meditation

lessons.title: Ren and the Dao
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius taught that a good life is humaneness practiced through ritual and family; the Daodejing taught that it is living simply in harmony with the Way, like water.
reading: A student asked Confucius (551–479 BCE) whether there was a single word to live by. The Master's answer, in James Legge's 1861 translation, is quoted below, and it is close to the Golden Rule stated in the negative. The Analects, sayings collected by his followers after his death, return again and again to one idea, *ren*, usually translated humaneness or benevolence. When another student asked about ren, Confucius said simply that it is to love people. Ren is the inner quality of a good person, and the Analects spend most of their pages on how it is formed.

It is formed, Confucius taught, through *li*, ritual and proper conduct, and through xiao, filial devotion. Xiao is the respect a child owes to parents and ancestors. A person learns to be humane at home, by serving parents, and carries that care outward to the ruler, the friend and the stranger. The ideal is the *junzi*, the noble person, whose nobility comes from character rather than birth. Justice, for Confucius, is what follows when rulers are junzi. A ruler who is upright leads without needing to command. A state governed by virtue and ritual rather than by punishment produces people with a sense of shame who correct themselves.

The Daodejing, a short text attributed to Laozi and probably compiled around the fourth century BCE, reads almost like a reply. Confucius builds the good life from ritual, learning and role. The Daodejing warns instead that when the great *Dao*, the Way, is abandoned, people start talking about humaneness and righteousness. It praises *wu wei*, acting without forcing. Its favorite image is water, which benefits all things, does not compete, and settles in the low places that people avoid. The best ruler, it says, is one whose people barely know he exists.

Are these religions or philosophies? Scholars answer both. Confucianism has temples, rites for ancestors and a canon; Daoism developed priests, temples and practices for long life. In East Asia most people historically drew on both, along with Buddhism, without choosing. For the question on the board, the two give different answers within a shared world. Confucius: become humane through relationship and ritual, and justice will follow from good rulers. Laozi: let go of striving, return to simplicity, and the world will order itself.

ritual and proper conduct, through which Confucians believe humaneness is formed
the noble person of Confucian teaching, noble by character rather than by birth
the Way; in the Daodejing, the natural source and pattern of all things, which cannot be fully named

lessons.title: Seva and the Shared Meal
lessons.mainIdea: Sikh teaching answers both questions at once: a good life is honest work, remembrance of God and sharing, and justice is practiced daily in selfless service and the langar.
reading: Walk into any *gurdwara*, a Sikh house of worship, and after the prayer hall you will find a kitchen. In the *langar*, a free meal is cooked by volunteers and served to anyone who comes, without regard to religion, caste, wealth or gender. Everyone eats sitting in rows on the floor at the same level. The practice goes back to Guru Nanak (1469–1539), the founder of Sikhism. The later Gurus fixed it as a permanent feature of Sikh life. In the Chicago area, gurdwaras in Palatine and elsewhere serve langar every week to whoever arrives.

The langar embodies a teaching. Sikhs summarize the good life in three duties attributed to Guru Nanak. Naam japna is remembering God's name. Kirat karni is earning an honest living by one's own work. *Vand chhakna* is sharing what one earns with others. Sikhs believe in one God, formless and without rival, and hold that all people are equal before that God. The Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture that Sikhs treat as their living Guru, includes hymns of Hindu and Muslim saints as well as of the Sikh Gurus. Sikhs understand that choice as an expression of the same equality.

The word for selfless service is *seva*. Cooking in the langar, cleaning the shoes of visitors at the gurdwara door, and, in recent decades, running relief kitchens after floods and in refugee camps are all seva. Sikhs describe it as service done without desire for reward or recognition, offered to God through people. A well-known line attributed to Guru Nanak says that truth is high, but higher still is truthful living, and Sikh teachers often cite it to explain why the tradition measures a life by conduct rather than by belief alone.

Justice in Sikh tradition has an active edge. The tenth Guru, Gobind Singh, founded the *Khalsa* in 1699, a community of initiated Sikhs pledged to uphold righteousness and defend the oppressed. Sikh tradition remembers the ninth Guru, Tegh Bahadur, executed in Delhi in 1675, as giving his life to defend the religious freedom of others. Sikhs are a small tradition, perhaps twenty-five to thirty million worldwide. Yet the langar has become one of the most recognized answers on earth to the question of what justice looks like at a table.

the free community meal served at a gurdwara to all who come, eaten together at the same level
selfless service offered without desire for reward, central to Sikh life
sharing what one earns with others; one of the three duties Sikhs attribute to Guru Nanak
the community of initiated Sikhs founded by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699, pledged to righteousness

lessons.title: Ethics Without Scripture
lessons.mainIdea: Secular ethics answers the same questions by reason alone, through virtue, duty or consequences, and belongs in the comparison beside the religious answers.
reading: Marcus, the student with no sacred text, came back from the philosophy shelf with a real answer, and the comparison would be incomplete without it. Depending on the survey, between about a fifth and three in ten Americans, and more than a billion people worldwide, identify with no religion. Some of them hold that ethics needs no God at all; others simply reason about right and wrong without appealing to scripture. The chapter treats these views the way it treats every other column: describe, attribute, do not rank.

Three secular approaches have shaped Western thinking. Aristotle, writing in Athens in the fourth century BCE, taught that the good life is *eudaimonia*, flourishing. It is reached by practicing the virtues, stable habits such as courage, honesty and generosity, each a middle between two extremes. Immanuel Kant, in Germany in 1785, argued that morality rests on duty. Act only on a rule you could will everyone to follow, and always treat persons as ends, never merely as means. John Stuart Mill, in England in 1861, argued for *utilitarianism*. The right act is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number.

Notice how each maps onto the religious answers. Aristotle's virtues resemble Confucian self-cultivation and the Buddhist training of the mind. Kant's rule sounds like a philosophical version of the Golden Rule, though Kant himself insisted that his test was stricter and not the same. Mill's concern for the sum of happiness echoes the prophets' and the Qur'an's insistence that the poor count. The resemblances are real. So are the differences: a secular thinker grounds the answer in reason, experience or human nature, not in revelation, and does not connect it to God, karma or an afterlife.

Modern *humanism* gathers these threads into a stance. Human beings, it holds, can live ethically and find meaning through reason, compassion and responsibility to one another, without belief in the supernatural. The first Humanist Manifesto was published in 1933. Humanist groups today run ceremonies, chaplaincies and charities. For the question on the board, the humanist answer is that a good life is one lived thoughtfully and kindly in the one life a person can be sure of. Justice is what fair-minded people would agree to. Whether that is enough, or whether it borrows from the religions it sets aside, is itself a debate worth having in class, with both sides described fairly.

look.title: A Rule Everyone Could Follow

Lying to escape trouble fails the test, he argued, because if everyone lied when it helped them, no one would believe anyone, and lying would stop working. Compare the Golden Rule, Confucius's reciprocity and the Buddhist precept against false speech, each of which forbids the same lie for a different stated reason.

lessons.title: Where the Answers Meet and Part
lessons.mainIdea: The traditions converge on care for the vulnerable and a version of the Golden Rule, but they differ on the source of the rule, the nature of the self, and how justice relates to God.
reading: Now fill in the table. Read the six columns across, and the first thing you see is convergence. Nearly every tradition forbids killing, stealing and lying. Nearly every one commands care for the poor and the stranger: tzedakah, the Beatitudes, zakat, dana (Buddhist and Hindu giving), the langar. Nearly every one states a form of the Golden Rule: Leviticus, Matthew, the Analects, a saying of the Prophet Muhammad in the Hadith that one is not a believer until one wants for one's brother what one wants for oneself, and the Mahabharata's teaching not to do to others what would cause pain to oneself. Scholars call this the rule's near-universal reach.

Look more closely, and the reasons diverge. Why should I not hate my enemy? The Torah answers: because the LORD commands it and remembers Egypt. Matthew answers: because God sends rain on the just and the unjust, and the children should be like the Father. The Dhammapada answers: because hatred cannot end hatred, as a matter of how minds work. Confucius answers: because reciprocity is the rule of a humane person. Kant answers: because you could not will a world of hatred. The same conduct, five different foundations. A student who reports only the conduct has missed the most interesting part.

The deepest difference concerns the self. The Abrahamic traditions speak of a single person, created by God, who lives once, is judged and is answerable. Hinduism speaks of an eternal atman that passes through many lives, and Sikhism of a soul that passes through births until it merges with God. Buddhism denies a permanent self altogether and grounds ethics in the reduction of suffering wherever it arises. Confucianism locates the person in a web of relationships. These are not small variations. They change what a good life is for, and they change what justice is owed to, whether a soul, a stream of experience, an ancestor or a citizen.

A second difference concerns God. In the Torah, the Gospels and the Qur'an, justice is what God demands and God will finally establish. In Buddhism and Confucianism no such lawgiver stands behind the rule, and in secular ethics none is needed. Yet a Muslim, a Buddhist and a humanist may work side by side in the same food pantry on the same Saturday morning in Chicago, each with a full account of why. The study of religion does not ask which account is true. It asks you to be able to state all of them accurately, in their own words, and to notice, with respect, that they are not the same.

giving or generosity, a core virtue in Hindu and Buddhist teaching
in Hindu teaching, the eternal self that passes through many lives
reports of the words and actions of the Prophet Muhammad, second in authority to the Qur'an for Muslims

Analects Book XV
review.why: Leviticus 19:18 closes with "I am the LORD," placing the command's authority in God. Matthew, the Dhammapada and the Analects ground their teachings differently.

review.q: What did the prophet Amos say about crowded festivals in a kingdom that cheated the poor?
choices: They should be held more often
God despised them; justice should flow like a stream instead
They should move to Jerusalem
They were the only thing that pleased God
review.why: Amos 5:21–24 has God reject the feasts and demand judgment like water and righteousness like a mighty stream, because the poor were being crushed.

review.q: Which of these belongs to the Sermon on the Mount?
choices: The Five Pillars
The Eightfold Path
The Beatitudes
The three duties of Guru Nanak
review.why: The Beatitudes open Matthew 5. The Pillars are Islamic, the Path is Buddhist, and the three duties are Sikh.

review.q: What does zakat require of a Muslim with savings above a threshold?
choices: Fasting for one month
A pilgrimage to Mecca
Reciting the shahada daily
Giving a fixed yearly share, commonly 2.5 percent, to the poor
review.why: Zakat is the pillar of required giving. Fasting, pilgrimage and the shahada are separate pillars.

review.q: In the Gita, what does Krishna tell Arjuna about the fruits of action?
choices: Act from duty and release attachment to the reward
Refuse to act until the reward is guaranteed
Never act at all
Give all rewards to the priests
review.why: Karma yoga: one has a right to action, never to its fruits. Krishna warns equally against inaction.

review.q: Which pair correctly matches a term to its tradition?
choices: Ren: Buddhism
Seva: Sikhism
Dharma: Confucianism
Metta: Judaism
review.why: Seva is Sikh selfless service. Ren is Confucian humaneness, dharma is Hindu duty, and metta is Buddhist loving-kindness.

review.q: How does Confucius's version of the rule of reciprocity differ from Matthew 7:12?
choices: Confucius states it positively and Matthew negatively
They are word for word the same
Confucius states it negatively (do not do) and Matthew positively (do)
Confucius rejects reciprocity entirely
review.why: The Analects say what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others; Matthew says whatever you would have others do to you, do to them.

review.q: What is the deepest point of difference among the traditions' ethical answers, according to the chapter?
choices: Whether lying is wrong
Whether the poor deserve help
Whether the Golden Rule exists
What the self is and whether a lawgiving God stands behind justice
review.why: The traditions converge on conduct such as care for the poor. They diverge on the nature of the self and on whether justice rests on God's command.

chapters.title: What Happens When We Die? Why Is There Suffering?
chapters.bigQuestion: How do the world's traditions explain death and suffering, and how do their answers shape the way people grieve?

story.title: After the Funeral
story.kicker: Four cousins leave their grandmother's funeral with the same loss and four different sets of words for it.
paragraphs: The funeral Mass for Grandma Rosa was held at a parish on Chicago's Southwest Side, the church where she had been baptized, married and, for sixty years, a Sunday regular. The priest spoke of the resurrection and of a life that had not ended but changed. Her rosary was placed in her hands in the casket. Afterward the family drove to the cemetery, and then everyone crowded into her small brick house, where the neighbors had already covered the kitchen table with food.

The four oldest cousins ended up on the back porch. Daniela, who still went to Mass with her parents, said she was sure Grandma was with God. Noah, whose father is Jewish, said his dad's family would be sitting shiva for a week if this were their funeral, with the mirrors covered and people bringing meals. He was not sure what his father's side believed happened after death, and he realized he had never asked.

Anjali's mother is Hindu, and Anjali had been to her grandfather's cremation in India two summers before. She remembered the priest, the fire and the ashes carried to the river. Her mother had told her that the soul does not die, that it moves on to another life the way a person changes clothes. Sam, who had grown up with no religion, said quietly that he thought Grandma was simply gone. What he could not stop thinking about was the last two years, when she had been in pain almost every day.

That was the question that silenced them. Why had someone so kind suffered so long? Daniela said Grandma had offered her pain to God and kept her rosary in the hospital. Anjali said her mother would talk about karma, though not as a punishment. Noah remembered a rabbi at his cousin's bar mitzvah saying that the Book of Job was written for exactly this question and never fully answers it. Sam said maybe there was no reason at all.

Nobody won the argument, and nobody tried to. Late in the evening an aunt came out with plates of cake and said that Grandma would have liked seeing them talk. The cousins had just done, without a textbook, what this chapter asks you to do: put the answers side by side, attribute each to its tradition, and notice where they meet and where they part.
story.think: Each cousin reached for words from a tradition, or from none. Why might the words a family uses at a death matter so much to the people left behind?

lessons.title: Judaism: This World and the World to Come
lessons.mainIdea: The Hebrew Bible focuses on life in this world, while later Jewish tradition taught resurrection and the world to come, and Jewish movements still differ on how to understand them.
reading: Most of the Hebrew Bible says little about life after death. The dead go down to *Sheol*, a shadowy place of silence, and the Psalms ask whether the dead can praise God at all. The Torah's promises of blessing and punishment concern this life: long days in the land, children, harvests. For much of ancient Israel, a person lived on through descendants, through the people and through a good name.

Near the end of the biblical period the picture changes. The Book of Daniel, which most scholars date to the second century BCE, contains the Hebrew Bible's clearest statement of *resurrection*, the dead rising to life again, quoted below. By the first century CE Jews disagreed about it. The Pharisees taught resurrection. The Sadducees, the priestly party, rejected it because they found it nowhere in the Torah. The rabbis who shaped later Judaism followed the Pharisees.

Rabbinic tradition speaks of *Olam Ha-Ba*, the world to come, where the righteous receive their reward. Maimonides, the great twelfth-century scholar, included resurrection of the dead among his Thirteen Principles of Faith. The traditional daily prayer praises God, who gives life to the dead. Many rabbinic sources describe Gehinnom as a place of purification rather than endless punishment, often lasting no more than twelve months.

Modern movements read these teachings differently. Orthodox Jews generally affirm bodily resurrection. Classical Reform Judaism, in its 1885 Pittsburgh Platform, set bodily resurrection aside in favor of the immortality of the soul, and many Reform and Reconstructionist Jews today speak more of memory, legacy and the soul than of a future rising. Across all of them, Jewish teaching tends to keep the emphasis on this life: on keeping the commandments now, not on speculating about what comes after.

words.d: in the Hebrew Bible, the shadowy place of the dead, where all go after death
the dead being raised to life again, in body, at the end of time
Hebrew for the world to come; in rabbinic Judaism, the life or age of reward after this one

look.title: Those Who Sleep in the Dust
look.text: And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
look.prompt: The verse calls death sleep and resurrection waking. What does that image suggest about how its author thought of death? Why might a verse like this matter to Jews living under persecution, as most scholars think Daniel's first readers were?

check.q: How does most of the Hebrew Bible describe the place of the dead?
choices: As Sheol, a shadowy place of silence
As a paradise garden for the righteous
As a cycle of rebirth into new bodies
As a place of fire for all sinners
check.why: Most of the Hebrew Bible speaks of Sheol, a dim place of the dead, and places reward and punishment in this life.

check.q: Why did the Sadducees reject resurrection?
choices: Because Maimonides had rejected it
Because they found it nowhere in the Torah
Because they believed in rebirth instead
Because the Pharisees had banned it
check.why: The Sadducees, the priestly party, accepted only what they found in the Torah, and they did not find resurrection there.

check.q: What did the Reform movement's 1885 Pittsburgh Platform do with bodily resurrection?
choices: It made it the center of Jewish belief
It required all Reform Jews to affirm it daily
It set it aside in favor of the immortality of the soul
It moved it from the Talmud into the Torah
check.why: Classical Reform Judaism, in the Pittsburgh Platform, set aside bodily resurrection and spoke instead of the soul's immortality.

lessons.title: Christianity: The Empty Tomb
lessons.mainIdea: Christians believe that Jesus rose from the dead and that his resurrection promises the resurrection of all, followed by judgment and eternal life, though churches differ on the details.
reading: One of the earliest Christian writings on death is a letter. Around 55 CE Paul wrote to the church in Corinth, where some doubted that the dead would rise. His answer, in 1 Corinthians 15, is that everything depends on one event. If Christ has not been raised, he writes, the faith is empty. Christians believe that Jesus was crucified, buried and raised on the third day, and they celebrate that event each year at *Easter*.

For Christians, Jesus's resurrection is the first of many. Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of those who have died, and he describes a resurrection body that is transformed, no longer subject to decay. The Nicene Creed, recited in many churches every Sunday, ends by looking for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. Christians teach a final *judgment*, pictured in Matthew 25, where the nations are judged by how they treated the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner.

Most Christians believe that at death the soul goes to God, awaiting the final resurrection. Heaven is described as life in God's presence and hell as separation from God. Branches differ here. Roman Catholic teaching includes *purgatory*, a state of purification for those who die in God's grace but not yet fully cleansed. Catholics pray for the dead for that reason. Protestant churches rejected purgatory at the Reformation, and Orthodox Christians pray for the dead without defining purgatory as Catholics do.

Christians also differ on who will be saved and on how literally to take the images of fire and gold streets. Some hold that only those who explicitly trust in Christ are saved. Others hope that God's mercy may reach further. What they share is the conviction, stated in the Gospel of John and quoted below, that death is not the last word because of what they believe happened on Easter morning.

words.d: the Christian festival celebrating the resurrection of Jesus from the dead
in Christian, Jewish and Muslim teaching, God's final assessment of each person's life
in Roman Catholic teaching, a state of purification after death for those who die in God's grace

look.title: I Am the Resurrection
look.text: Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:
look.prompt: Jesus says this to Martha before raising her brother Lazarus. Compare it with Daniel 12:2. Where does each text place the hope of resurrection: in an event at the end of time, in a person, or in both?

check.q: According to Paul in 1 Corinthians 15, what does Christian faith depend on?
choices: The building of the Temple
The Ten Commandments
Good deeds outweighing bad ones
The resurrection of Christ
check.why: Paul writes that if Christ has not been raised, the faith is empty; the resurrection is the event everything rests on.

check.q: In Matthew 25, by what are the nations judged?
choices: By how they treated the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner
By how many prayers they said
By which language they spoke
By whether they kept the Sabbath
check.why: In Matthew 25 the nations are judged by their care for the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner.

check.q: Which Christian branch teaches purgatory as a defined state of purification?
choices: Protestant churches
Roman Catholic teaching
All Christian churches equally
No Christian church
check.why: Purgatory is Roman Catholic teaching; Protestants rejected it at the Reformation, and the Orthodox do not define it the same way.

lessons.title: Islam: The Day of Judgment
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe that after death each soul waits in the barzakh until the Day of Judgment, when all are raised, their deeds weighed, and they enter paradise or hell.
reading: When a Muslim dies, the body is washed, wrapped in plain white cloth and buried quickly, usually within a day, facing Mecca. Muslims do not cremate. The plain shroud is the same for rich and poor. It expresses a belief the Qur'an repeats on nearly every page: every person will return to God and give an account. Belief in the Last Day is one of the six articles of faith that Sunni Muslims list, alongside belief in God, angels, scriptures, prophets and God's decree.

The Qur'an calls the life to come *akhira*, the hereafter, and sets it against dunya, this present world. Between death and the end, according to Islamic teaching, the soul waits in the *barzakh*, a barrier or interval. Then comes the Day of Resurrection. The Qur'an describes the earth shaking and giving up its dead, the sky splitting, and every person raised in body to face judgment. Early suras of Mecca describe these scenes in vivid, rhythmic language.

On that day, according to the Qur'an, deeds are weighed on a scale, and each person receives a record of what they did. Sura 99, one of the shortest, says that whoever has done an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever has done an atom's weight of evil will see it. The righteous enter *jannah*, the garden, described with rivers, shade and peace. The wicked enter jahannam, the fire. The Qur'an stresses throughout that God is merciful and that no soul bears another's burden.

Muslims differ on some details. Scholars have debated whether punishment in jahannam is eternal for all who enter it, and many hold that believers who sinned may be purified and then brought out by God's mercy. Sufi writers often dwell on the soul's longing to meet God more than on the scales. Shia and Sunni Muslims share the core teaching on resurrection and judgment. What stands out in comparison is how closely Islam ties the hereafter to daily life: each prayer, each gift of zakat, each act of honesty is recorded.

words.d: Arabic for the hereafter, the life after death that the Qur'an sets against this present world
in Islamic teaching, the interval in which the soul waits between death and the Day of Resurrection
Arabic for the garden; paradise in the Qur'an

look.title: An Atom's Weight
look.text: In its own words, a short sura describes the earth shaking violently and giving up its burdens, and people asking what has happened to it. On that day people come forward in groups to be shown their deeds. Anyone who has done good the weight of the smallest particle will see it, and anyone who has done evil the weight of the smallest particle will see it.
look.cite: Qur'an, Sura 99 (al-Zalzala, The Earthquake), paraphrased; compare Rodwell (1861) and Palmer (1880)
look.prompt: The sura says even the smallest deed will be seen. How might that belief shape the way a Muslim thinks about an ordinary afternoon? Compare it with Matthew 25.

check.q: How is a Muslim body usually prepared and buried?
choices: Cremated, with ashes placed in a river
Kept at home for forty days
Washed, wrapped in a plain white cloth and buried quickly facing Mecca
Placed in a family tomb above ground with jewels
check.why: Muslims wash and shroud the body in plain cloth and bury it quickly facing Mecca; Islam does not permit cremation.

check.q: What is the barzakh in Islamic teaching?
choices: The scale on which deeds are weighed
The garden of paradise
The final fire
The interval in which the soul waits between death and resurrection
check.why: The barzakh, meaning barrier or interval, is where the soul waits between death and the Day of Resurrection.

check.q: What does Sura 99 teach about deeds?
choices: Even an atom's weight of good or evil will be seen on the Day
Only very great deeds are remembered
Deeds do not matter if one says the right words
Deeds are erased at death
check.why: Sura 99 says that anyone who has done an atom's weight of good or evil will see it on the Day of Judgment.

lessons.title: Hinduism: The Soul Changes Clothes
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus believe the atman passes through many lives in samsara, shaped by karma, until it reaches moksha, release from rebirth.
reading: At the burning ghats of Varanasi, on the banks of the Ganges, cremation fires burn day and night. Many Hindus hope to die in Varanasi or to have their ashes placed in the Ganges, a river they regard as holy. A Hindu funeral, *antyesti*, usually ends in cremation, often lit by the eldest son. Rites for the dead continue for about ten to thirteen days, varying by region and community, and families later offer food and prayers for their ancestors in rites called shraddha.

The belief behind the fire is that the body dies but the self does not. Hindu texts call the true self the *atman*. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that the self is never born and never dies, and that it casts off worn-out bodies as a person casts off worn-out clothes, as shown below. The atman moves through *samsara*, the cycle of birth, death and rebirth, taking many forms across many lives.

What shapes each new life is karma, the principle that actions have consequences that follow a person, in this life and the next. Good actions lead to better births; harmful ones to harder births. Karma in this sense is not a judge's sentence. Hindu teachers describe it more like a law of nature, the way a seed produces its own kind of plant. It explains, in this view, why lives begin in such different circumstances.

The goal is not endless rebirth but release from it, called *moksha*. Hindu paths describe moksha differently. For the Advaita Vedanta school, it is realizing that atman is Brahman, the one ultimate reality, like a drop recognizing it is the ocean. For many devotional traditions, devoted to Vishnu, Krishna or Shiva, it is an eternal life of love in God's presence. Both views agree that death is a passage, not an end, and that how one lives now shapes where the passage leads.

words.d: in Hindu thought, the true, eternal self or soul
the cycle of birth, death and rebirth taught in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh traditions
in Hindu thought, liberation from the cycle of rebirth
the Hindu funeral rite, the last sacrifice, usually ending in cremation

look.title: Worn-Out Clothes
look.text: Krishna tells Arjuna that just as a person throws away worn-out garments and puts on new ones, so the embodied self throws away worn-out bodies and enters new ones. Weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it and wind cannot dry it. It is eternal and unchanging.
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 2.22–24, paraphrased; compare Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial (1885)
look.prompt: Krishna uses this image to comfort a warrior afraid of killing his relatives. Why might the same image comfort a grieving family at a cremation? What does the image assume about what a person really is?

check.q: What happens to the atman at death, according to many Hindus?
choices: It ends forever with the body
It sleeps in Sheol until the end of time
It is weighed on a scale and sent to the garden
It passes on to a new body, as a person changes clothes
check.why: The Gita teaches that the atman casts off worn-out bodies and takes new ones, moving through samsara.

check.q: How do Hindu teachers usually describe karma?
choices: As a law of consequences, like a seed producing its own plant
As a judge's sentence handed down after death
As a prayer said at funerals
As the name of the river at Varanasi
check.why: Karma is described as a natural law of consequences, not a judge's verdict.

check.q: How does Advaita Vedanta describe moksha?
choices: As rebirth into a royal family
As realizing that atman is Brahman, like a drop knowing it is the ocean
As waiting in the barzakh
As the resurrection of the body
check.why: Advaita Vedanta teaches that liberation is realizing the self's identity with Brahman, the one ultimate reality.

lessons.title: Buddhism: Rebirth Without a Soul
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists teach rebirth driven by karma but deny a permanent self that passes from life to life, and the goal is nirvana, the ending of the cycle.
reading: Buddhists share the picture of samsara with their Hindu neighbors, but with a striking change. The Buddha taught *anatta*, non-self: there is no permanent, unchanging soul inside a person. What we call a self is a changing stream of body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness. So what is reborn? A Buddhist text called the Questions of King Milinda answers with an image of a lamp lit from another lamp. The flame is neither the same flame nor a different one.

What carries over, Buddhists teach, is the momentum of karma, intentional action and its results. A life shaped by craving, hatred and delusion tends toward rebirth in painful conditions; a life shaped by generosity, kindness and wisdom toward better ones. Traditional Buddhist cosmology describes several realms of rebirth, including humans, animals, hungry ghosts, hell beings and gods. None of them is permanent, and even the heavens eventually end.

The goal is to stop the cycle altogether. *Nirvana* means blowing out, as a flame goes out when its fuel is gone. The fuel, in Buddhist teaching, is craving. A person who reaches nirvana is not reborn at death. The Buddha declined to describe what that state is like in ordinary terms, and Buddhist schools have explained it in different ways. Theravada teachers stress the ending of suffering. Many Mahayana traditions add paths such as rebirth in the Pure Land of the Buddha Amitabha.

Buddhist funerals reflect these teachings. Monks chant texts on impermanence, and families make offerings and gifts in the name of the dead to transfer merit to them. In Tibetan Buddhism, the Bardo teachings describe a passage of up to forty-nine days between death and rebirth. Many East Asian families hold memorial rites every seven days through the forty-ninth day. The verse below, from Max Müller's translation of the Dhammapada, is often recalled at such times.

words.d: the Buddhist teaching of non-self: there is no permanent, unchanging soul
in Buddhism, the blowing out of craving and the end of rebirth and suffering
in Buddhism, the good results of wholesome actions, which can be dedicated to others, including the dead

look.title: All Created Things Perish
look.text: 'All created things perish,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way that leads to purity.
look.cite: Dhammapada, verse 277, translated by F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10 (1881)
look.prompt: Müller's older English says passive in pain; many modern translators say the person grows weary of suffering or turns away from it. How could knowing that all things perish help a grieving person, according to this verse?

check.q: What does the Buddhist teaching of anatta deny?
choices: That karma has results
That suffering exists
That there is a permanent, unchanging soul
That the Buddha taught at all
check.why: Anatta, non-self, denies a permanent soul; a person is a changing stream of body and mind.

check.q: Which image explains Buddhist rebirth in the Questions of King Milinda?
choices: A soul changing clothes
A seed sleeping in the dust
A drop returning to the ocean
A lamp lit from another lamp
check.why: The Questions of King Milinda uses a flame passed from lamp to lamp, neither the same nor different.

check.q: What does nirvana literally mean?
choices: Blowing out, as a flame goes out
Rising again, as the sun rises
Crossing a river
Returning home
check.why: Nirvana means blowing out; craving, the fuel of rebirth, is extinguished.

lessons.title: Jainism and Sikhism: Two Paths to Release
lessons.mainIdea: Jains teach that the soul frees itself from karmic matter through strict nonviolence, while Sikhs teach that liberation comes through God's grace and remembering God's name.
reading: Jainism, the tradition taught by Mahavira in the sixth or fifth century BCE, has the most physical picture of karma in Indian religion. Jains hold that every living being has a *jiva*, an eternal soul, by nature pure and all-knowing. Karma, in Jain teaching, is a fine kind of matter that sticks to the soul through passions such as anger, greed and pride and through harmful action. Weighed down by it, the jiva is reborn again and again.

Liberation comes by stopping new karma and burning off the old. That is why Jains practice ahimsa, nonviolence, with such care, avoiding harm even to insects, and why they value fasting and meditation. A soul entirely freed of karma rises to the top of the universe and dwells there in endless knowledge and bliss. Jains call such liberated souls siddhas. Near the end of life, some devout Jains take a vow of *sallekhana*, gradually giving up food with the approval of their community and teachers. Jains describe it as a peaceful, conscious death, and its practice has been debated in Indian courts.

Sikhism, founded by Guru Nanak (1469–1539), also teaches rebirth driven by karma. But in Sikh teaching, karma is not the last word; God's grace is. Liberation, called *mukti*, comes when a person, by God's grace, remembers the divine Name, lives truthfully and serves others. The self then merges with God, as Sikhs describe it, like water joining water. Sikhs stress that mukti can be experienced in this life, not only after death.

Sikh funerals reflect this. The body is usually cremated, the evening hymn Kirtan Sohila is recited, and the ashes are placed in running water. The family often arranges a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib over the following days. Sikh teaching discourages loud wailing, since death is understood as the will of God and a return to God. Both Jains and Sikhs, then, share samsara and karma with Hindus and Buddhists but draw very different maps of the way out.

words.d: in Jainism, the eternal soul present in every living being
a Jain vow near the end of life of gradually giving up food, undertaken with community approval
in Sikhism, liberation from rebirth through God's grace, bringing union with God

look.title: Two Ways Out of the Cycle
look.text: A Jain nun sweeps the path ahead of her with a soft brush so she will not step on insects, and she eats only before sunset. A Sikh volunteer rises before dawn to recite prayers, then spends the morning cooking in the langar. Both believe in rebirth and karma. Both are working toward release.
look.prompt: Explain what each woman believes she is doing about karma. Which one relies more on her own effort, and which one on grace? Use the terms jiva and mukti.

check.q: How does Jainism describe karma?
choices: As a fine matter that sticks to the soul through passions and harmful acts
As God's decision about each person
As an illusion with no effect
As a festival held after a death
check.why: Jain teaching treats karma as a subtle matter that clings to the jiva and weighs it down.

check.q: In Sikh teaching, what brings mukti?
choices: Strict fasting alone
God's grace, with remembering the Name, truthful living and service
Being born into the right family
Visiting Varanasi at death
check.why: Sikhs teach that liberation comes through God's grace as a person remembers the Name and lives truthfully.

check.q: What do Jains and Sikhs share with Hindus and Buddhists?
choices: Belief in a single judgment day
Burial facing Mecca
Belief in samsara and karma
The practice of sallekhana
check.why: All four traditions teach rebirth shaped by karma, though they describe release in different ways.

lessons.title: The Ancestors Remain
lessons.mainIdea: In many African and Chinese traditions the dead become ancestors who stay connected to the living, who honor them and ask for their help.
reading: In early April, many Chinese families go to the cemetery for *Qingming*, the Tomb-Sweeping Festival. They clear weeds, repair the grave, set out food and tea, burn incense and paper offerings, and bow. In many homes an altar holds wooden tablets bearing ancestors' names, and families light incense there on important days. Honoring ancestors in this way is older than Confucius, and Confucian teaching made it central to xiao, filial devotion.

*Ancestor veneration* rests on the idea that the dead continue as members of the family. They are remembered, fed and consulted, and in turn they watch over the living. Chinese popular religion also recognizes spirits with no one to care for them. During the Ghost Festival in the seventh lunar month, families make offerings for these neglected dead. Confucius himself was reserved about the spirit world. When asked about death, he answered that one who does not yet understand life can hardly understand death.

Many African traditions hold a similar picture. Among the Yoruba of West Africa, ancestors are honored at family shrines and, in some communities, in Egungun festivals, where masked dancers are understood to embody the returning dead. Libations, pourings of water or drink on the ground, are offered to ancestors in many African societies. The Kenyan scholar John Mbiti described recently departed ancestors as the living-dead: still remembered by name, still part of the household.

In these traditions death does not end a relationship; it changes it. The ancestor's role depends on being remembered, which makes the living responsible for the dead, and the dead for the living. Scholars note that such traditions often focus less on a final judgment than on the ongoing health of the family and community. Many Christians, Muslims and Buddhists in Africa and East Asia also keep forms of ancestor remembrance, blending older practices with their faith in varied ways.

words.d: honoring deceased family members, who are believed to remain connected to and care for the living
the Chinese Tomb-Sweeping Festival in early April, when families tend graves and honor ancestors
a pouring of water or drink as an offering, often to ancestors

look.title: A Table for the Dead
look.text: At a Chinese American family's home in Chicago's Chinatown, a small altar holds photographs of grandparents, a bowl of oranges, three sticks of incense and a cup of tea that is refilled each morning. At a Yoruba family's shrine, a daughter pours water on the ground and speaks her father's name before asking for his blessing on her new job.
look.prompt: What do both families seem to believe about the dead? How is this different from a view in which the dead go far away to be judged?

check.q: What do Chinese families do at Qingming?
choices: Fast for thirty days
Scatter ashes in a holy river
Read the Guru Granth Sahib in full
Clean graves and offer food, incense and bows to ancestors
check.why: Qingming is the Tomb-Sweeping Festival, when families tend graves and honor their ancestors.

check.q: What did John Mbiti mean by the living-dead?
choices: Recently departed ancestors still remembered by name and part of the household
People who have reached nirvana
Souls waiting in Sheol
Spirits punished in hell
check.why: Mbiti used the term for ancestors who are still remembered and treated as members of the family.

check.q: How did Confucius answer a question about death?
choices: He described heaven in detail
He said one who does not understand life can hardly understand death
He said the soul is reborn
He refused to honor ancestors
check.why: In the Analects, Confucius turns the question back to life, saying one must first understand life.

lessons.title: Job and the Whirlwind
lessons.mainIdea: The Book of Job rejects the idea that suffering is always punishment, and God's answer from the whirlwind points to the limits of human understanding.
reading: The Book of Job opens with a man who is blameless and upright. In a single day he loses his herds, his servants and his ten children. Then his body breaks out in sores. His first response, quoted below, is famous. But then Job sits in the ashes for seven days in silence with three friends, and when he finally speaks, he curses the day he was born. The book that follows is one of the most searching treatments of suffering in world literature.

Job's friends offer the standard explanation. God is just, they say, so suffering must be punishment for sin; Job should confess and be restored. Job insists he has done nothing to deserve this and demands a hearing with God. The book takes Job's side against the friends. At the end, God says that the friends have not spoken rightly, as Job has. The question of how a good and powerful God can allow suffering is called *theodicy*, and Job refuses the easy answer.

When God finally answers, it is from a *whirlwind*, and not with an explanation. Instead God asks Job a long series of questions. Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Can you command the morning, or feed the lion? The speech paints the vastness of creation, far beyond human understanding. Job answers that he has spoken of things too wonderful for him. His fortunes are then restored.

Readers have never agreed on what the ending means. Some Jewish and Christian readers find in it trust: suffering is real, but the world's order is beyond human sight. Others note that Job is never told why he suffered, and they take the book as permission to protest to God. Jewish thinkers after the Holocaust returned to Job for exactly that reason. What most readers agree on is that Job refuses to blame the victim.

words.d: an attempt to explain how a good and all-powerful God can allow evil and suffering
the storm from which God speaks to Job at the end of the Book of Job
a prayer or poem of grief and complaint addressed to God

look.title: The LORD Gave

look.prompt: These are Job's first words after losing everything, but by chapter 3 he is cursing the day he was born and uttering a lament. Why might the book include both responses? What does that say about grief?

A Jewish mourning rite
A book of the Qur'an

lessons.title: The Cross and the Test
lessons.mainIdea: Christians believe God entered suffering in Jesus on the cross, while the Qur'an teaches that hardship is a test met with patience and trust in God.
reading: Christianity places a symbol of suffering at its center: the *cross*, on which, the Gospels say, Jesus was executed by Roman authorities. Christians believe that in Jesus God did not stand apart from human pain but entered it. The Gospels record him weeping at a friend's tomb and crying out from the cross in the words of Psalm 22, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Many Christians take comfort in the belief that God knows suffering from the inside.

Christians also read suffering in the light of the resurrection. Paul writes that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to come (Romans 8:18). The Book of Revelation ends with a vision, quoted below, of a world in which God wipes away every tear. Christians differ on why suffering exists at all. Some stress human free will; others, God's mystery. Many say that the cross does not explain suffering but shows God sharing it.

The Qur'an speaks of suffering as a *test*. It says God created death and life to test which people are best in deed (67:2). It tells believers that they will be tested with fear, hunger and loss of wealth, lives and crops. Then it gives good news to the patient, who say when disaster strikes: we belong to God, and to God we return (2:155–156). Muslims around the world say those words, in Arabic, on hearing of a death.

The virtue asked of the believer is *sabr*, patience, steadfast endurance with trust in God. The Qur'an also says that God does not burden any soul beyond what it can bear (2:286). Muslims do not read hardship as a sign that God has abandoned a person; the prophets, according to a well-known hadith, were tested most of all. In comparison, Christianity and Islam agree that suffering is not meaningless and not the last word. They differ on whether God suffers: Christians say God did so in Christ, while Islamic teaching holds that God is beyond all suffering.

words.d: the Roman instrument of execution on which Christians believe Jesus died; the central Christian symbol
in the Qur'an, a trial of hardship or ease through which God shows a person's faith and deeds
Arabic for patience; steadfast endurance with trust in God

lessons.title: The First Truth and Karma
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhism begins by naming suffering as a fact of life, and karma explains much suffering in Indian traditions, though teachers warn against using it to blame the suffering.
reading: A young mother named Kisa Gotami, according to a Buddhist story, carried her dead child from house to house, begging for medicine. At last she came to the Buddha. He told her to bring a mustard seed from a household where no one had ever died. She went door to door. Every family had lost someone. By evening she understood that death comes to all. She laid her child to rest and became a nun.

The story illustrates the Buddha's *First Noble Truth*: life as ordinarily lived involves dukkha, suffering or unsatisfactoriness. Birth, aging, sickness and death are dukkha; so is being separated from what one loves. The Buddha did not ask why a creator would allow this, because Buddhism does not teach a creator God. Instead the Second Truth names suffering's cause, craving, and the Third and Fourth teach that it can end and how.

In Hindu, Buddhist and Jain thought, karma explains why suffering falls where it does. Actions have results, and some results ripen in later lives. That can make suffering seem less random: it has a cause, even when the cause cannot be seen. Hindu teachers add that suffering met with patience and devotion can purify the soul. For many believers the idea brings comfort, because in this view the universe is not unjust.

Teachers in all three traditions also warn against misusing karma. In one Buddhist sutta, the Buddha tells a questioner that not every painful feeling comes from past karma. Some come from bodily illness, the change of seasons, careless living or harm done by others. Modern Hindu and Buddhist teachers, and reformers who fought caste discrimination, have argued that karma must never be used to blame the poor or the sick or to excuse cruelty. The compassionate response, all three traditions teach, is to help. Here karma and Job meet: both warn against blaming the one who suffers.

words.d: the Buddha's teaching that ordinary life involves dukkha, suffering or unsatisfactoriness
Pali for suffering, stress or unsatisfactoriness
action and its consequences, which in Indian traditions shape this life and future lives

look.title: The Mustard Seed
look.text: Kisa Gotami asks for a cure and receives an errand. The Buddha does not bring her child back or explain why the child died. He sends her out to learn something she could not have learned by being told. When she comes back, her grief has not vanished, but it has changed.
look.prompt: What did Kisa Gotami learn at the doors that the Buddha could not simply tell her? Compare the Buddha's response with God's answer to Job from the whirlwind. What is similar about how each teacher refuses a direct explanation?

check.q: What was Kisa Gotami told to bring the Buddha?
choices: A mustard seed from a house where no one had died
A lamp lit from another lamp
A garment of plain white cloth
An offering of tea for the ancestors
check.why: The Buddha asked for a mustard seed from a household that had known no death, so that she would learn death comes to all.

choices: Because it teaches that suffering does not exist
Because Buddhism does not teach a creator God
Because the Buddha forbade questions
Because the Qur'an already answers it
check.why: Buddhism does not teach a creator God, so the question becomes what causes suffering and how it ends.

check.q: What warning do teachers give about karma?
